# OPENING: Did Christ have a biological father?

**Position.** No. Jesus had no human biological father. He was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, and Joseph was his father only by legal and reputed standing. By "biological father" I mean a man who contributed to the generation of the child.

---

## 1. The genealogy changes its verb at Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2-16 runs on one formula: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob…" Verse 16 then breaks it: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, **of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ**."

**[L2]** The verb throughout is ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat, fathered"). In verse 16 the relative pronoun is ἧς (hēs, "of whom"), **feminine singular**. It can only refer to Mary, not to Joseph. The verb becomes the passive ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born"). Joseph is called ἀνήρ (anēr, "husband"), not the one who begat.

**[L4]** From [L1] Matthew 1:16 and [L2] the feminine ἧς, the evangelist who wrote "begat" thirty-nine times withheld it at the one point where it would make Joseph the father. The break is deliberate.

## 2. The stated source of the conception is the Holy Ghost

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, **before they came together**, she was found with child **of the Holy Ghost**." Verse 20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** τὸ γεννηθὲν (to gennēthen, "that which is begotten/conceived") is qualified by ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου (ek pneumatos estin hagiou, "is out of Holy Spirit"). The preposition ἐκ (ek, "out of") names the source.

**[L1]** Luke 1:34-35: "How shall this be, seeing I **know not a man**?" The answer is: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: **therefore also** that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** οὐ γινώσκω (ou ginōskō, "I do not know") uses the biblical idiom for sexual relations. The overshadowing is ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "will cast a shadow over"). The causal link is διὸ καί (dio kai, "for which reason also"), so the child's identity as Son of God follows from the manner of conception.

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1, "Adam **knew** Eve his wife; and she conceived" (Hebrew יָדַע, yadaʿ, "to know"), fixes the idiom. Mary's question asks how conception could occur without it. The angel does not correct her premise. He supplies a different agent.

## 3. Joseph is "supposed," not named, as father

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "Jesus… being (**as was supposed**) the son of Joseph." Matthew 1:19: Joseph "was minded to put her away privily." Matthew 1:25: Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L2]** ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was reckoned, was thought") describes a reputation, not a fact. Joseph's plan to divorce fits only if he knew he was not the father. The angel's reassurance in Matthew 1:20, "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife," presupposes the same.

**[L3]** Luke 2:48-49 shows the same gap. Mary says, "thy father and I have sought thee." The child answers, "wist ye not that I must be about **my Father's** business?" He corrects who his Father is.

## 4. The prophetic and genealogical chain requires it

**[L1]** Genesis 3:15: "the **seed of the woman**." **[L2]** The Hebrew זֶרַע (zeraʿ, "seed") is ordinarily reckoned through the male, yet here it is attributed to the woman alone. Isaiah 7:14, quoted in Matthew 1:23, reads: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child." Matthew's Greek is παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin, unmarried maiden"). Isaiah's Hebrew is עַלְמָה (ʿalmāh, "young woman of marriageable age"), and Matthew's Spirit-given rendering fixes the sense.

**[L1]** Jeremiah 22:30 says of Coniah: "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David." Matthew 1:11-12 places Jechonias (the same king) in Joseph's line.

**[L3]** Luke 3:31 traces a line through Nathan, not Solomon's line through Jechonias. Romans 1:3 says Christ was "made of the seed of David according to the flesh," and Galatians 4:4 says he was "made of a woman," γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "come into being out of a woman").

**[L4]** From [L1] Jeremiah 22:30 with Matthew 1:11-12, and [L3] Luke 3:31 with Romans 1:3, Christ's right to David's throne cannot rest on Joseph's blood. A blood-descent from Joseph through Jechonias would fall under the bar. David's seed "according to the flesh" must come through the mother, which is consistent with Galatians 4:4 and Hebrews 10:5, "a body hast thou prepared me."

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on:

1. Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" formula at Joseph, using the feminine ἧς (hēs, "of whom") so that Jesus is "born" of Mary and not begotten by Joseph. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:2-16; [L2] ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat") against ἧς and ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born").
2. The source of the conception is stated as the Holy Ghost, before Joseph and Mary came together. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18, 20 and Luke 1:34-35; [L2] ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Holy Spirit"), οὐ γινώσκω (ou ginōskō, "I do not know"), and διὸ καί (dio kai, "therefore also"); [L3] Genesis 4:1 for the idiom of "know."
3. Joseph stands as father only by reputation and legal standing. Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23, Matthew 1:19 and 1:25; [L2] ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was supposed"); [L3] Luke 2:48-49, where the child names a different Father.
4. The prophetic and genealogical requirements are met only through the woman, not through Joseph's blood. Footing: [L1] Genesis 3:15, Isaiah 7:14 and Jeremiah 22:30 with Matthew 1:11-12; [L2] זֶרַע (zeraʿ, "seed") and παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin"); [L3] Luke 3:31, Romans 1:3 and Galatians 4:4.
5. Therefore Christ had no human biological father: he was conceived of the Holy Ghost in Mary, "made of a woman." Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35; [L2] ἐκ (ek, "out of") and γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "come into being out of a woman"); [L3] Hebrews 10:5, "a body hast thou prepared me."

# CHALLENGE: Did Christ have a biological father?

**Answer: Yes. Joseph — named, of the house of David.** The genealogy, the town, the disciple, the narrator and the mother all name him, and the seed the promise requires is a seed proceeding out of a man's body. I press each link below.

---

## Against LINK 1 (Matthew 1:16)

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16 as printed: *"And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."* The verse states **who bore** the child. It does not state who begat him; it does not say "Joseph begat him not."

**[L2]** The passive ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born") with ἧς (hēs, "of whom") is a statement of **birth**, and birth runs from the mother. Non-narration of a begetting is not the denial of one.

**[L1]** The whole register before v.16 runs on the father's name — *"Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob"* — and the angel opens by naming Joseph inside that register: *"Joseph, thou son of David"* (Matthew 1:20).

**[L3]** Reckoning in Israel is **by the father's house**, and the register is struck when the father's house cannot be shown: *"By their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers"* (Numbers 1:2); *"they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers"* (Numbers 1:18). In Ezra 2:59 those who *"could not shew their father's house"* are put from the priesthood, and in 2:61-62 priests *"called after the name"* of a wife's house are *"as polluted, put from the priesthood."*

**[L4]** (footing: [L1] Matthew 1:20 "thou son of David" beside the father-name register; [L3] Numbers 1:2, 18 and Ezra 2:59-62) — the genealogy runs through Joseph **because** the reckoning is by the father's house. A break in the verb formula at v.16 is not stated by the text to mean Joseph did not beget; that reading is imported. **LINK 1 does not carry its conclusion.**

---

## Against LINK 2 (the Holy Ghost)

**[L2]** ἐκ (ek, "out of") with God or Spirit in the New Testament names **covenant origin**, never biological paternity: *"born of God"* (John 1:13; 1 John 3:9; 5:1), *"is of God"* (1 John 4:7) — all spiritual. Where Paul means flesh he marks it: *"made of the seed of David **according to the flesh**"* (Romans 1:3). **[L1]** Matthew 1:20 has no such flesh-mark.

**[L2]** The two verbs of Luke 1:35 denote **presence and power**, not begetting. The Holy Ghost shall **come upon** (ἐπέρχομαι, eperchomai) thee — the same word at *"after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you"* (Acts 1:8), spoken to the twelve. **[L3]** *"the Spirit of the LORD came upon David"* (1 Samuel 16:13) is anointing. The **overshadowing** (ἐπισκιάζω, episkiazō) is the presence cloud — *"a cloud overshadowed them"* (Mark 9:7); *"his shadow"* (Acts 5:15). Neither verb at any row denotes a begetting.

**[L1]** The conclusion of that verse is a **title**: *"shall be **called** the Son of God"* — and the same title is given to Solomon, who had a father: *"I will be his father, and he shall be my son"* (2 Samuel 7:14), said to David *"Solomon **thy son**... I have chosen him to be **my son**"* (1 Chronicles 28:6). **[L3]** *"this day have I begotten thee"* (Psalm 2:7) is applied at the **resurrection** (Acts 13:33). The title does not decide the question of a biological father.

**[L1]** The angel's ground for taking her is the child's covenant claim, not a report of no man: *"fear not to take unto thee **Mary thy wife**: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost"* (Matthew 1:20) — *"I will be his father, and he shall be my son"* (2 Samuel 7:14). **[L1]** The canon's stated means of begetting stands: *"Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived"* (Genesis 4:1). **LINK 2 asserts a source the verse's own idiom does not state.**

---

## Against LINK 3 (Joseph "supposed")

**[L1]** Four registers name him father — Mary: *"thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing"* (Luke 2:48); the narrator: *"the parents brought in the child Jesus"* (Luke 2:27), *"his parents went to Jerusalem"* (2:41); the town: *"Is not this the son of Joseph?"* (Luke 4:22), *"Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know"* (John 6:42); a disciple: *"Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph"* (John 1:45). Mary is the recipient of the annunciation, and she says *"thy father"* — and that word is never corrected in the text.

**[L2]** νομίζω (nomizō, "to deem, to be wont") carries no verdict of its own. Its other rows show it: *"supposing him to have been in the company"* (Luke 2:44 — wrong); *"where prayer **was wont** to be made"* (Acts 16:13, the same verb form ἐνομίζετο, enomizeto). Context decides each row.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19 states intent and two grounds — *"a just man, and not willing to make her a public example"* — and no verb of knowledge appears in the row. **[L1]** *"knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son"* (Matthew 1:25) **bounds** the abstinence to the pregnancy; the word is *"till"* (ἕως οὗ, heōs hou).

**[L1]** Luke 2:49 is a title over a trade — *"I must be about my Father's business"* — set beside *"thy father and I"* in the same scene; it names the covenant Father (1 Chronicles 28:6) and does not unname Joseph the husband. **LINK 3 reads a reputation word as a verdict the text does not give it.**

---

## Against LINK 4 (the prophetic chain)

**[L1]** The **Davidic** seed is anatomical and male — *"which shall proceed out of **thy bowels**"* (2 Samuel 7:12); *"Of the fruit of **thy body** will I set upon thy throne"* (Psalm 132:11); *"of the fruit of **his loins**, according to the flesh"* (Acts 2:30); *"made of the seed of David **according to the flesh**"* (Romans 1:3); *"it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda"* (Hebrews 7:14).

**[L2]** *"her seed"* (Genesis 3:15, זֶרַע, zeraʿ, "seed") is the woman-word in the offspring sense at four rows (Genesis 3:15; 16:10; 24:60; Isaiah 54:3) and **none of them is Davidic**. The Davidic promise is attached to the man's body.

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14's word is עַלְמָה (almah, "young woman"); the virgin-word בְּתוּלָה (bethulah, "virgin") is a different word and is not used there. **[L1]** the sign is bounded in Isaiah's own lifetime: *"before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good"* (7:16), and *"the child"* is born at 8:3-4, after which *"O Immanuel"* stands at 8:8 — in Isaiah's day.

**[L1]** Jeremiah 22:30 read whole: *"Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper **in his days**: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more **in Judah**."* **[L1]** the sons of Jeconiah are named (1 Chronicles 3:17-18), and the signet plucked at Jeremiah 22:24 is **set** on Zerubbabel (Haggai 2:23), *"governor of Judah"* (Haggai 1:1) — not king. **[L1]** Jeremiah's own rule: *"If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil"* (18:8). **[L3]** the name Iechonias appears twice in the New Testament (Matthew 1:11-12) and **the curse is never cited against Christ**.

**[L1]** *"made of a woman"* (Galatians 4:4) is the mortality idiom — *"How then can man be justified with God? and how can he be clean that is born of a woman?"* (Job 25:4) — and it is said of John the Baptist, *"Among them that are born of women"* (Matthew 11:11), whose father is named (Luke 1:13, 63). **"Of a woman" excludes no father.** **LINK 4's conclusion — that the flesh seed "must come through the mother" — is contradicted by the seed rows and by the reckoning rule, and Mary's own descent is nowhere stated** (Luke 1:36 gives her a kinswoman, *"of the daughters of Aaron"*).

---

## Against LINK 5 (the keystone)

**[L1]** *"made of the seed of David according to the flesh"* (Romans 1:3); *"of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh"* (Acts 2:30); *"it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda"* (Hebrews 7:14).

**[L2]** Acts 2:30's "loins" is ὀσφύς (osphys) — the same word as *"he that receiveth them... of the house of Levi, who receiveth tithes... **out of the loins of Abraham**"* (Hebrews 7:5, 9-10): descent through the man's body.

**[L1]** Joseph is the man the text names: *"Joseph her husband"* (Matthew 1:19); *"Mary thy wife"* (1:20); *"Joseph, thou son of David"* (1:20); *"thy father and I"* (Luke 2:48); *"of the house and lineage of David"* (Luke 2:4); *"the throne of his father David"* (Luke 1:32). **[L3]** the law calls a betrothed woman *"his neighbour's wife"* (Deuteronomy 22:24), and to part he must *"put her away"* (Matthew 1:19).

**[L4]** (footing: [L1] the seed rows of Romans 1:3, Acts 2:30, Hebrews 7:14, 2 Samuel 7:12; [L2] ὀσφύς = loins, the descent-word; [L3] Genesis 4:1 and Deuteronomy 22:24) — the promised seed proceeds out of a man's body, and the canon's stated means of begetting is the husband knowing his wife. Joseph is the husband from the espousal; *"knew her not till she had brought forth"* bounds the abstinence to the pregnancy. **The child is of his loins.** The keystone "no human biological father" cannot stand beside *"of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh."*

---

## UNSUPPORTED [L4] PREMISES (defender's own words, verbatim)

1. **D1** — *"the evangelist who wrote 'begat' thirty-nine times withheld it at the one point where it would make Joseph the father. The break is deliberate."* No text states that a passive verb denies a begetting; the father's-house reckoning (Numbers 1:2, 18; Ezra 2:59-62) says the opposite about registers.
2. **D4** — *"Christ's right to David's throne cannot rest on Joseph's blood... David's seed 'according to the flesh' must come through the mother."* Contradicted by 2 Samuel 7:12 ("out of thy bowels"), Acts 2:30 ("fruit of his loins, according to the flesh") and by the reckoning by the father's house; and no row gives Mary a David descent.
3. **D4** — the Jechonias bar, standing on Jeremiah 22:30, while the row reads *"in his days"* and *"in Judah,"* Jeremiah 18:8 bounds pronounced sentences, and the canon never applies this curse to Christ (Matthew 1:11-12).
4. **D5** — *"Therefore Christ had no human biological father"* — set beside *"of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh"* (Acts 2:30) and *"thy father and I"* (Luke 2:48). This is the premise the seed rows will not carry.

# ROUND 2: DEFENDER'S ANSWER

The challenger's method is to take each link alone and say "the verse doesn't state it." The case is the chain, so I re-seat each term in its chain below.

---

## Link 1: Matthew 1:16 does not stand alone

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2-16 has thirty-nine occurrences of "begat" (ἐγέννησεν, egennēsen, "fathered"), the last being "Jacob begat Joseph." The fortieth step reads: "Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus." The challenger says non-narration is not denial. But the denial is not left to the grammar alone. Verses 18-20 follow at once: "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise." The word γέννησις (gennēsis, "origin, generation") introduces the account of how, and the account names no man.

**[L2]** ἧς (hēs, "of whom") is feminine singular. The relative pronoun could have been masculine had the writer wished to attach the child to Joseph. Matthew chose the grammar that cannot.

**[L3]** The challenger cites Numbers 1:2, 18 and Ezra 2:59-62 to show reckoning is by the father's house. I agree that this is the rule of registers, and it is the reason Matthew keeps Joseph in the register. Joseph is the legal head through whom the child is "son of David" (Matthew 1:20), and the angel addresses him as such because he must take the child in. Ezra 2:61 also works against the challenger: a man "took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai… and was called after their name." Israel's own register allowed a man to be named after his wife's house.

**[L4]** Footing: [L1] the formula running thirty-nine times and then changing, plus Matthew 1:18-20; [L2] feminine ἧς against ἐγέννησεν. Chain: a formula that never varies and then varies at the single point where the sense would otherwise be fatherhood is a deliberate exception, and the following verses give the reason. I do not rest on the verb in isolation.

---

## Link 2: "of the Holy Ghost" in its chain

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18 says she was "found with child of the Holy Ghost" **"before they came together"** (πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν αὐτούς, prin ē synelthein autous, "before their coming together"). The challenger reads Matthew 1:25 as bounding Joseph's abstinence "to the pregnancy." Take that reading as given. It puts the pregnancy before the union, and 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not" (οὐκ ἐγίνωσκεν, ouk eginōsken, "was not knowing her") until the birth. **[L3]** That is the same verb the canon uses for begetting at Genesis 4:1, which the challenger himself calls "the canon's stated means of begetting." By that stated means, the text says Joseph did not use it before the child was born. So on the challenger's own reading of 1:25 and 1:18 together, the conception was not through Joseph.

**[L2]** The challenger says ἐκ (ek, "out of") with the Spirit means "covenant origin." The row is τὸ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν (to en autē gennēthen, "that which is begotten in her"), and ἐκ is applied to the thing **begotten in a womb**, not to a believer. In John 1:13 the "born of God" are set against "not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh." That is a contrast with fleshly begetting, which does not help the idea that Matthew 1:20 allows it.

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" (ἄνδρα, andra, "a man, a husband"). The question is about the **manner**. Verse 35 answers it: the Holy Ghost "shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: **therefore also** that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." **[L2]** διὸ καί (dio kai, "for which reason also") makes the title a **consequence of the conception**. Solomon's sonship in 2 Samuel 7:14 is a future covenant promise ("I will be"), with no "therefore." The challenger's parallel lacks the causal clause that Luke has. The overshadowing verb in Mark 9:7 is not asked to answer "how can this be?", while here it is the angel's whole answer to Mary's question.

---

## Link 3: "father" and "supposed"

**[L1]** Luke 3:23 is the narrator's own voice: "being (**as was supposed**) the son of Joseph." **[L3]** The same writer wrote Luke 1:34-35. He is not carelessly inserting a hedge in a genealogy, where a fact would be stated plainly.

**[L1]** The challenger lists the voices that say "father." Take them in context:
- **[L1]** The townspeople: "Is not this the son of Joseph?" (Luke 4:22). John 6:42 goes on: "whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?" These are voices of unbelief, wrong about origin, so they cannot adjudicate it.
- **[L3]** Mark 6:3: "Is not this the carpenter, **the son of Mary**?" The same crowd, with the mother named and no father.
- **[L1]** Luke 2:48-49: Mary says "thy father and I," and the child answers in the same scene, "wist ye not that I must be about **my Father's** business?" (τοῦ πατρός μου, tou patros mou, "of my Father"). The text sets the two titles side by side, and **[L1]** Luke 2:50-51 adds that they "understood not the saying which he spake" and "his mother kept all these sayings in her heart." Mary spoke the household title and did not understand the correction, which is what the narrative records.
- **[L3]** "Father" is also a forefather's title: "the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32), "our father Abraham" (Luke 1:73). So "father" proves no begetting.

**[L2]** Granted that νομίζω (nomizō, "to suppose, reckon") takes its verdict from context, as at Luke 2:44 and Acts 14:19, where the supposers are wrong. The context at Luke 3:23 is Luke 1:34-35.

---

## Link 4: the seed and the bar

**[L1]** Acts 2:30 says "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh." **[L2]** ὀσφύς (osphys, "loins") is the descent-word, but it names descent from David, not **through which parent**. **[L3]** Genesis 29:14, Laban to his sister's son Jacob: "Surely thou art my bone and my flesh." Flesh-kinship in Israel's own text runs through a mother. **[L1]** Romans 9:5: "of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came" (ἐξ ὧν, ex hōn, "out of whom," the Israelites), and no father is named.

**[L4]** Footing: [L1] Luke 1:35, "that holy thing which shall be born **of thee**"; [L1] Romans 1:3 and Acts 2:30, the flesh being David's; [L3] Genesis 29:14, flesh through a mother. Chain: if the child's flesh is David's flesh (Romans 1:3) and it came to him of Mary (Luke 1:35, Galatians 4:4, "made of a woman," γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός, genomenon ek gynaikos, "come into being out of a woman"), then Mary is of David's seed. The challenger says no row gives her a David descent. That is correct as a single statement, but the chain gives it.

**[L3]** Luke 3:23 reads "which was the son of Heli," while Matthew 1:16 has "Jacob begat Joseph." Two fathers for one Joseph. **[L3]** Ezra 2:61 (a man "called after their name"), Numbers 27:4-7 and 36:6-8 (daughters keeping the house within the tribe) fit Joseph reckoned in Heli's line through marriage. **[L4]** Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23 against Matthew 1:16, [L3] Ezra 2:61 and Numbers 36:6-8. Chain: two fathers named for Joseph are explained by a marriage-reckoning that the law already allowed. I mark this as a chain inference, not a stated fact.

**[L1]** Jeremiah 22:30 in full: "Write ye this man childless (עֲרִירִי, ʿărîrî, 'stripped of heirs'), a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah." The challenger reads "in his days" over both clauses. The second clause begins with its own "for" and is general ("no man of his seed"). **[L1]** The challenger's own proofs fit the bar: Zerubbabel (Haggai 1:1, "governor of Judah") held a signet but no throne. **[L1]** Jeremiah 18:8 is conditioned on turning, and the text records no turning by Coniah after 22:28. Matthew places Jechonias in Joseph's line (1:11-12), and it is **Matthew who also writes 1:16 with ἧς**. The challenger says the curse is never cited against Christ. The grammar of 1:16 is the answer: the register gives the legal title through Joseph and withholds the begetting at the single point that would bring a descendant of Jechonias onto the throne. That is a reading of Matthew's own construction, not an argument from silence.

**[L2]** Isaiah 7:14, עַלְמָה (ʿalmāh, "young woman of marriageable age"): **[L3]** Genesis 24:43 uses the same word of Rebekah, whom 24:16 calls "a virgin, neither had any man known her" (בְּתוּלָה, bethulah, "virgin"). So the word is used of one who is a virgin. **[L1]** The child of Isaiah 8:3 is named Maher-shalal-hash-baz, not Immanuel. **[L1]** Isaiah 8:8 has "thy land, O Immanuel," addressed to a ruler of the land, and 9:6 says "unto us a child is born… The mighty God." The sign at 7:14 is given to "the house of David" (7:13), the very house in question.

---

## Link 5: the keystone

**[L4]** Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18, 20, 25 and Luke 1:34-35; [L2] ἐκ with γεννηθέν, and διὸ καί; [L3] Genesis 4:1 and 29:14. Chain: the conception was before the union (1:18), Joseph did not know her until the birth (1:25), the angel answers Mary's "I know not a man" with the Spirit's power and a causal "therefore" (Luke 1:35), and the flesh-kinship to David can pass through a woman. The challenger's "of his loins" requires Joseph to have been the begetter, which is exactly what Matthew 1:16 and 1:18-25 deny.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN (updated)

1. Matthew 1:16 breaks a thirty-nine-fold "begat" formula with feminine ἧς (hēs, "of whom"), and verses 18-20 give the account of the birth.
2. The conception is "of the Holy Ghost" before they came together, and Joseph "knew her not" until the birth (Genesis 4:1 idiom). Luke 1:35 gives the causal "therefore."
3. Joseph is father "as was supposed" (Luke 3:23). The household and crowd voices are answered by Luke 2:49 and Mark 6:3.

> Matthew 1:25 — *"And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."*

The abstinence clause **follows the taking**. It bounds the marriage after the taking to the birth: *"till"* (ἕως οὗ, heōs hou). It does not reach backward over the espousal **[L4]** (footing: [L1] the sequence of 1:24-25; [L2] the imperfect οὐκ ἐγίνωσκεν, ouk eginōsken, "was not knowing," a state clause in sequence after the verb "took").

The verb συνέρχομαι (synerchomai, "come together") names married union elsewhere — *"Come together again"* (1 Corinthians 7:5) — and Matthew sets what came together by what follows: *"took unto him his wife"* (1:24), her coming into his house.

Inside that sequence the record's reading stands **[L4]** (footing: [L1] *"Joseph her husband,"* Matthew 1:19; *"Mary thy wife,"* Matthew 1:20; *"till,"* Matthew 1:25; [L3] *"his neighbour's wife"* of a betrothed damsel, Deuteronomy 22:24; *"Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived,"* Genesis 4:1) — **Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal.** No row narrates any knowing then; no row denies it; and the begetting is nowhere narrated at all. I have chosen him to be my son"* (1 Chronicles 28:6); *"I will be his father, and he shall be my son"* (2 Samuel 7:14) **[L3]** (Psalm 2:7 "this day have I begotten thee" applied at the **resurrection**, Acts 13:33). **[L1]** Jeremiah 22:30 read whole: *"Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah"* — and the sons of Jeconiah are **named** (1 Chronicles 3:17-18), and the signet is **restored** to Zerubbabel (Haggai 2:23), *"governor of Judah"* (Haggai 1:1), not king. **[L3]** The name appears twice in the New Testament (Matthew 1:11-12) and the curse is never cited against Christ; Jeremiah's own rule bounds pronounced sentences (18:8).
